opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really common misreading, and I think it's worth being careful about. The time-horizon number is something like: on our task suite, here's the length of task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human expert to do it, at which the model succeeds about 50% of the time. So there are a few big caveats packed in there.

First, 50% is a coin flip. If you're thinking about delegating real work, you probably care about a much higher reliability threshold, and the horizon at 80% success is substantially shorter. So "it can do anything that takes you 12 hours" is wrong even on our own tasks. It's more like: on 12-hour tasks, it gets roughly half of them.

Second, the distribution of tasks matters a lot. Our suite is mostly software engineering, ML engineering, cybersecurity-type tasks, things that are well-specified, can be automatically scored, and live in a fairly self-contained environment. Real jobs are messier. You have ambiguous goals, you need context that lives in people's heads, you coordinate with colleagues, there's no clean scoring function telling you whether you're done. We've seen evidence that on messier tasks, models do noticeably worse relative to their clean-benchmark performance. So I'd expect the effective horizon on your actual job to be shorter, possibly a lot shorter, depending on how much of it looks like our tasks.

Third, the human baseline. "Twelve hours" means twelve hours for a reasonably skilled professional who's new to that specific task, not someone with years of context on your codebase. Someone deeply embedded in a project can often do things much faster, so the comparison to "your job" shifts again.

That said, I don't want to overcorrect. The point of the metric isn't "here's exactly what it can do for you"; it's a fairly robust way of tracking the trend. The striking thing is how consistently that horizon has been growing, doubling every several months. Even if the absolute number overstates usefulness for your particular job, the slope tells you something real about where this is heading, and that's what I'd pay most attention to.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a 12-hour task as measured against a skilled professional new to that task, but does not say a human contractor may take weeks to complete someone’s own job task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that interpretation is basically wrong, and it's one of the misreadings we worry about most. The time-horizon metric is a pretty specific thing. We take a set of tasks, we measure how long they take skilled human baseliners, and then we look at the task length at which the model succeeds roughly fifty percent of the time. So a "12 hour" number means that on our task suite, at the 50 percent success threshold, the model is reliably handling things that took our humans around twelve hours. It does not mean it can do everything that takes you twelve hours. At the 50 percent point it's failing half the time, by construction. If you look at the 80 percent reliability horizon, it's typically a lot shorter, maybe four or five times shorter.

And then there's the question of what our tasks actually look like. They're mostly software and research-adjacent, they're well-specified, they have a clean automatic scoring mechanism, they don't need you to go talk to someone to find out what the real requirement is, and they're not embedded in a messy codebase that's accumulated ten years of context. Those are all things that make tasks easier for models relative to humans. So a twelve-hour task in your actual job, which probably involves ambiguous requirements and tacit knowledge and some amount of "wait, why is this broken" detective work, is not the same thing as a twelve-hour task in our suite. We try to be really explicit about this in the write-ups, that the number is a measurement of one thing and the extrapolation to "your job" is a separate claim that we are not making.

What I do think the number tells you is something about the trend. The reason we care about it is less the absolute value and more that it's been doubling on a fairly consistent schedule, and if you believe that continues, then the gap between "handles our clean tasks" and "handles your messy tasks" might close faster than people's intuitions suggest. So I'd say don't read it as a statement about today's capability in your job, read it as a trend line, and then do your own checking about how far your work is from the kind of thing we're measuring.

r001.rationale: The response says a 12-hour task in someone’s actual job is not equivalent to a task in the benchmark, but it does not state that a human contractor may take weeks to complete it.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a pretty misleading interpretation. A time horizon isn’t a claim that the model can do anything in your job that takes you 12 hours. It’s a summary of how it performs on a particular distribution of tasks, with task length measured by how long those tasks take a human. If we’re talking about a 50% time horizon, that means roughly a 50% probability of success at that duration—not reliable completion of everything shorter than that.

And human completion time is only one predictor of difficulty for a model. Something that takes you 12 hours because there’s lots of fairly straightforward coding could be much easier for it than a short task that requires context you haven’t written down, or navigating an ambiguous situation with other people.

So I’d read the number as evidence about the length of tasks models can handle in the setting we’re testing. Translating that into what fraction of your job they can do requires knowing what your job actually involves, what information and tools the model gets, and how reliable you need it to be.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human completion time as one measure of task difficulty, but it does not say that a 12-hour task in someone’s job may take a human contractor weeks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a pretty misleading interpretation. The time horizon is a measure of the difficulty of tasks the model can complete at a particular success rate, where difficulty is measured by how long those tasks take a human. It isn’t saying that the model can do any arbitrary task that takes you twelve hours, or that it can reliably replace twelve hours of your work.

The tasks we evaluate are much more constrained than a whole job: you have a fairly clear objective, you have the relevant environment, and you can assess whether the task was completed. A lot of real work involves figuring out what the objective should be, getting context from other people, and making judgments where success is much harder to specify.

And the success rate matters enormously. If you’re quoting a fifty-percent time horizon, that means succeeding about half the time on tasks of that difficulty in the evaluation distribution. That’s useful evidence about capabilities, but it’s quite a different claim from ‘anything in your job that takes twelve hours.’

r001.rationale: The response discusses human task duration and model time horizons, but does not state that a 12-hour task in someone’s job may take a human contractor weeks to complete.
